content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.

There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.

content.content:
# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:

         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable

     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.

type of a program's own may, or is a numeral type itself.
The declared type of a variable, a field or a parameter, and the declared
return type of a functional, are such places, the parameter types of the
declaration that a call invokes among them (\secref{resolving-coercion}).
There the numeral is converted into that type, from its exact value:
so \EXP{q\COLON\mathbb{Q} = 0.1} binds the rational \EXP{1/10},
\EXP{r\COLON\mathbb{R}64 = 0.1} the floating-point number nearest to it, and
\EXP{n\COLON\mathbb{N}32 = 5} the natural number 5.
It is a static error if the numeral's value lies outside the range of that
type, or rounds to an infinity there.
Where nothing fixes a type, as where a variable is declared without a type, or
a parameter has the type \TYP{Any}, \TYP{Object} or \TYP{Number} or a type
parameter declared without a bound, the numeral is converted into its
\emph{default}: a numeral without a radix point into \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or into
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value does not fit in the
narrower type, and a numeral with a radix point into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
So \EXP{x = 3} binds \VAR{x} as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
\EXP{\VAR{bigN} = 3000000000} binds \VAR{bigN} as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{y = 0.5} binds \VAR{y} as an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64};
\EXP{x \sequiv z} is \VAR{true} for \EXP{z\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = 3};
and for \EXP{\KWD{object}\;\TYP{Cell}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)},
\EXP{\TYP{Cell}(3)} is a \EXP{\TYP{Cell}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket}.
\secref{numeral-default} says where else a numeral takes its default, as where
several numerals fix one type parameter, and how a numeral whose conversions
tie is read.
The default applies to a numeral, and to a static expression of numerals once
it is folded (\secref{static-expr}), never to an expression of a numeral type.

A type of a program's own receives a numeral through its own coercion from the
numeral's type, such as \EXP{\KWD{coerce}(x\COLON\TYP{RadixPointNumeral})},
whose body reads the four numbers.
A numeral at a place whose type is a type of a program's own that declares no
coercion from the numeral's type is a static error: coercion does not chain
(\secref{coercion}), so the numeral is not converted into its default first.
The coercion sees the four numbers of a numeral as written: a negative constant
reaches it as the prefix operator \EXP{-} applied to the coercion's result for
the natural numeral (\secref{static-expr}), so a type without that operator
refuses it.
At each place where such a numeral stands, the coercion is applied once, not at
each evaluation of the place, so that the numeral there denotes one object, as
a string literal does: two evaluations of one place yield the same object, and
each place has its own application of the coercion.
A numeral type is written in a program only as the type of a parameter, of a
coercion or of an operator, never as the type of a variable, a field or a
functional's result, nor as a static argument; so the constants \VAR{pi} and
\VAR{e} of \library\ are values of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
Inside the body of a coercion, two values of a numeral type are equal, and
strictly equivalent, when their values $v/r^m$ are equal: there \EXP{2.5} and
\EXP{2.50} are strictly equivalent, and so are \EXP{0.1_{2}} and \EXP{0.5}.
\revision{revival-numerals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 said that
numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types, and so gave a
numeral where nothing fixes a type its own type.
The revival decided on 8~November 2026 that a numeral is converted where it
stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type, and elsewhere into the
default above; that a type of a program's own receives a numeral only through
its coercion from the numeral's type, once for each place; and that the numeral
types are written only as parameter types.
The text this replaces, the revival's own of 29~September 2026
(\secref{revival-numeral-type}), named the type of an integer numeral
\TYP{IntLiteral}, the name that the compiled path's own library gives it.}

numeral's type is refused, since coercion does not chain; the alternative not
taken converts it into its default first and then by the type's own coercion

So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` (P-40). The numerals' 24 bindings, `IntLiteral`'s 21 and `FloatLiteral`'s 3, leave the library with those two types (P-174), so no carrier is designed for them; `IntLiteral`'s other 8, its conversions and comparisons, are Fortress text over its `asZZ` (F-331). A test on both paths holds the two halves together where both run. Why: every array, vector, varargs list and `args` of the one library is built on `PrimitiveArray` or `PrimImmutableArray`, and a body left on glue compiles to the library's own `builtinPrimitive`, which fails, so by the code's reading a compiled program would raise at its first array; walk's loader carries no element, `Thread` or literal (F-299), and an `Object` carrier would take walk's array writes out of walk's transactions. Detail: `reviews/natives-device-2026-11-07.md`, sections 3.1 to 3.4; the store's shape: `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-28.md`, "The questions for the curator, before the launch", Q2.
91:- P-76 **An integer numeral has the Working Draft's type `NaturalNumeral` (P-174), which each of the eight number types converts from: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32`.** Where nothing fixes a type it is a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit (P-173). `NaturalNumeral` takes the place of `IntLiteral`, the name that the compiler's prelude and the interpreter's library give the type, and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic goes, since an expression of numerals alone folds before the checker (P-173). content.content: 105:- P-174 **A numeral's own type is the Working Draft's, `NaturalNumeral` or, with a radix point, `RadixPointNumeral`, both below `Numeral`, and its value carries the Draft's four numbers as fields; a program's own number type receives a numeral through its coercion from that type, which the compiler calls once per class, when the class loads.** The four numbers are the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r`, and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`); they are fields of the value, not static parameters of the type, and the Draft's explicit-radix variants and `Literal[\v\]` fold into the radix field. The two types replace the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). A numeral type is written only as a parameter type, of a coercion or an operator, never as a variable's, field's or return type, so the library's `pi` and `e` (`Library/Constants.fsi:16-17`) are `RR64`. A program's type declares the coercion inside itself, such as `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, and reads the four numbers; the compiler emits the call with the numbers as constants, so a numeral at a program's type denotes one object per site, as a string literal does (P-171): in his words, "Coerce is just invocation of the numeric type constructor that gets the constants from the parser." A program's type with no coercion from the numeral type refuses a numeral. Inside a coercion's body two numeral values compare by their reduced value, so `2.5` and `2.50` are equal there, under `SEQV` too (P-168). Fields cannot make a size static, so the design contradicts the binary chapter's static word width from a numeral's digit count (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1621`, `:1659-1662`), for Appendix I, and drops its `opr ||` with a numeral. Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`literals.tex:141-145`), as an interval type should receive `3.1415926535897932384` unrounded (`:135-141`). The team built that coercion under its own names, with the exact value in the numeral ("ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec", commit `128f313b5b`, 2009), but never the four numbers, and no team word calls the names temporary or final; the design keeps what they built, one type for each kind of numeral with its exact value at the coercion, and adds the Draft's names and numbers. The team's one word on a numeral's value at run time: "IntLiterals should always be transient objects with minimal lifetime" (`compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java:21-23`, 2009). A coercion handed a double loses: a bfloat16 type then rounds `1.00390625000000000001` twice, to `0x3F80`, where one rounding gives `0x3F81`. P-173 weighs the bend of P-26. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1, 3 and 6; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`, sections 6 and 7.

\end{enumerate}

\Library\ declare none of the constant traits.
An expression composed only of numerals and operators is folded, before the
static check and on both implementations, into a \emph{signed constant}, which
holds its value exactly and whose kind its operands give: computed from
numerals without a radix point and without a quotient, it is an integer,
written as an integer numeral or a negated one; computed from numerals without
a radix point with a quotient among its operations, it is a quotient, written as
the reduced quotient of two integer numerals; and computed from a numeral with a
radix point, it is written as a numeral with a radix point, or a negated one,
where its denominator divides a power of ten, and otherwise as the reduced
quotient of two numerals whose numerator has a radix point.
Where nothing fixes the type of a signed constant (\secref{literals}), an
integer takes the default of an integer numeral, a quotient the type
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and a constant computed from a numeral with a radix point the
type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, whatever its value, so that \EXP{6/3} is a
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{0.5 + 0.5} an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}; where a place fixes
a type, the constant is converted into it as a numeral is, with at most one
rounding.
So \EXP{2147483647 + 1} is the \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} \EXP{2147483648},
\EXP{-2147483648} is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{x = 7/2} binds the
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} \EXP{7/2}, and \EXP{0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3} is \VAR{true}.
----
If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
at most one floating-point rounding error.
But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
not just at compile time.

# Climb batch 29: the judge's ruling on the merged-diff review

The merged-diff review of climb batch 29 (heads `1d50c6bbbf` before it and `6a654baa13` after its corrections, base `b430f9f428`) did not approve the merged tree. It raised two blocking findings. Both concern rung T's Appendix I entry `revival-numerals` and the gather's box in `ranges.tex`, which claim more of walk than walk does on the merged tree. This file rules on the two findings and gives the repair. It does not rule on the review's two routed findings, which go to the next batch as the review filed them (`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`, "Climb batch 29, listed for his review").

## The standard

- The revision form makes the Effect of an Appendix I entry name "each departure: each way in which walk or the compiled path does not do what the new text says, with its ledger row" (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/specification.md`, "Changing the text: the revision form", item 1).
- Where a decision says which side is right and the wrong side is outside the work's area, the departure is recorded, and "if the passage has an Appendix I entry, name the departure or the conflict in the entry's effect, with its ledger row. Then the text claims no more than holds" (same file, "When the text and an implementation disagree").
- A changed sentence that says what walk or the compiled path does must be true of the tree (same file, the paragraph after item 4).

## Finding 1: a negative constant at a program's own number type

**Upheld.**

What the review claimed, and what holds:

- The text says a negative constant reaches a program's coercion "as the prefix operator `-` applied to the coercion's result for the natural numeral ..., so a type without that operator refuses it" (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:215-218`). This follows fork C6's default, "the judgement's repair 3, which he took" (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-29.md:369`). Right.
- Walk departs on the merged tree. Two rungs cause it together, and both causes are in the code:
  - rung F put the fold into walk's phase list (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java:130`, `INTEGERLITERALFOLDING` in `interpreterPhaseOrder`), so `-3` and `5 - 8` reach walk as one `IntLiteralExpr` of value -3;
  - rung N's site takes `x.getIntVal()`, signed, as the digit value, and counts the digits of the text with the sign stripped (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Numerals.java:160-179`).

  The review's probe at `1d50c6bbbf` (`bin/fortress walk`) printed 't 1 -3' for `t: Tally = -3` and for `t: Tally = 5 - 8`, and 'w 7' for `w: Written = -3`. The type declares no `-` and still takes the numeral. Right.
- The Effect names only the compiled half: "the compiled path gives a program's coercion a negative numeral with its sign, not as the prefix operator `-` on the coercion's result for the natural numeral (row~961)" (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5195-5197`). Walk's half, row 968, is missing. Right: the Effect breaks the revision form.
- The record side is done in `6a654baa13`: row 968 filed, and row 961 noting it ("Walk's half, through the same fold: row 968"). Right.

The way not taken is to make walk, the fold or the checker build the prefix minus. That is a code change, and the curator holds it as an open fork: PLAN item 75 lists "the fold keeps the operator's reference ...; the checker, and walk, build one; or rows 961 and 968 stand until the switch-over", with "No default on record beyond the fork's, which the landed tree departs from" (`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md:140`). Rung C reported its deviation from C6 as a point (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-numeral-checker/REPORT.md:135`, decision 8). Building the minus here would choose a way of an open fork for the curator, so the repair is the text only. Naming row 968 decides nothing on item 75. Either answer leaves the Effect true: a later fix removes the clause with its row.

## Finding 2: a size of 2^31 or more read as a value

**Upheld, and wider than the review found.**

What the review claimed, and what holds:

- P-173 says "a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` (P-40)". The text follows it (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:105-113`, the box).
- Walk reads such a size "as a `ZZ32` up to 2^31-1 and as a `ZZ64` above" (F-140, "A size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` is refused by the compiled checker ..."). F-140 held this before the batch. The review's probe at `1d50c6bbbf` printed 'big ZZ64 3000000000' for `sizeValue[\3000000000\]()`. Right: under walk such a size is not a `ZZ32`.
- The Effect's sentence "a \KWD{nat} parameter used as a value is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, ... (row~486)" (`changes.tex:5145-5148`) sits under "Both implementations ..." (`changes.tex:5127`). Its list of departures names only the compiled half of row 962, "stops with an error that no \KWD{catch} sees where a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter of $2^{31}$ or more is used as a value (row~962)" (`changes.tex:5197-5198`). Right: walk's half is missing.
- The gather's box says "the compiled type checker and the interpreter give a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a value the type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}" (`Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex:55-58`). This box is a changed sentence that says what walk does, and walk does not do it for a size of 2^31 or more. Right. The base's text already claimed "the interpreter makes it a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}" (the `ranges.tex` hunk of `4978a9b16e`), so the overclaim is older than this batch. It still has to be repaired here, because this batch rewrote the sentence.
- The record side is done in `6a654baa13`: row 962 now notes "Walk reads such a size as a ZZ64 (F-140): sizeValue[\3000000000\]() typed ZZ64 at 1d50c6bbbf". Right.

The review missed a third passage with the same claim. It is in `revival-inference`'s Rationale, which this batch rewrote: "Both implementations make a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a value a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{revival-numerals})" (`changes.tex:2237-2238`; the batch's diff adds this line). The repair qualifies all three passages.

Row 962 is `CONTESTED`: it leaves open whether such a read is refused where the class loads, raises `IntegerOverflow`, or is no `ZZ32`. The repair names the departure. It does not choose among those answers.

## The review's other work

The review committed only under `explorations/` (`git show --stat 6a654baa13`: seven files, all under `explorations/`). Its `fixed` and `fixesChecked` items cite their commits and runs. This ruling does not depend on them, and I did not check them again. No point to report holds the push, and this ruling adds none.

## Decision: repair

Both findings are settled by edits to `Specification/` only. No code, library, checker, interpreter or test file changes. Under the brief, an edit to the specification is a repair, not a landing on the gate. The edits change prose only. No example under `SpecData/` changes, so the gate's verdict on code, tests and `testSpecData` stands. The repair builds the specification once to check its LaTeX.

1. `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5191-5203` (`revival-numerals`, Effect, the list of departures). Replace the text from "the interpreter runs the operator of" through "(row~956)." with this:

   ```
   the interpreter runs the operator of
   \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} where a floating-point numeral stands to the left of an
   \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} (row~958), and counts only one of the leading zeros of a
   numeral with a radix point among its digits (row~960); the compiled path
   keeps a numeral's own type at the selector of a \KWD{typecase} (row~963);
   both give a program's coercion a negative constant with its sign, not as the
   prefix operator \EXP{-} on the coercion's result for the natural numeral, so
   that a type without \EXP{-} takes it: the compiled path as a negative numeral
   (row~961), and the interpreter, which folds the constant as the compiled path
   does, as a natural numeral of negative value, whose digit count is that of
   the numeral without its sign (row~968); where a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
   parameter of $2^{31}$ or more is used as a value, the compiled path stops
   with an error that no \KWD{catch} sees, and the interpreter makes it a
   \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} (row~962); and both leave an expression of numerals alone
   as written where the form of its result needs a prefix \EXP{-} or a \EXP{/}
   that its component writes nowhere (row~956).
   ```

   Keep "The implementations depart from the text in these further ways, each with its row of the revival's gap ledger:" before it. This settles finding 1, and finding 2 at `:5145-5148`: that sentence stands, and the list now names both halves of row 962. Row 968's claim is the source for the interpreter's clause (`explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, row 968), and row 962's notes for the `ZZ64` clause.

2. `Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex:55-58` (the gather's `\revision{revival-inference}` box). Replace

   ```
   run it: the compiled type checker and the interpreter give a \KWD{nat} or
   \KWD{int} parameter used as a value the type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}
   (\secref{revival-numerals}).}
   ```

   with

   ```
   run it: the compiled type checker and the interpreter give a \KWD{nat} or
   \KWD{int} parameter used as a value the type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}
   (\secref{revival-numerals}), the interpreter only where the size is below
   $2^{31}$, since it makes a larger one a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} (row~962 of the
   revival's gap ledger).}
   ```

   This follows the form of the boxes that cite a row in `Specification/basic/inference.tex:261` and `:283`.

3. `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:2237-2238` (`revival-inference`, Rationale). Replace

   ```
   Both implementations make a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a value a
   \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{revival-numerals}), where the compiled type checker
   ```

   with

   ```
   Both implementations make a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a value a
   \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{revival-numerals}), the interpreter one whose size
   is below $2^{31}$ (row~962 of the revival's gap ledger), where the compiled type checker
   ```

   Then rewrap that line to the file's width. Keep the rest of the sentence ("gave it the type of a numeral before 8~November 2026, ...").

4. Grep `Specification/` (not `Specification-1.0-frozen/`) for any other changed sentence that says both implementations give a size used as a value a `ZZ32`, or that names row 961 without row 968: `grep -rn 'used as a value\|row~961' Specification --include=*.tex`. The hits that state a decision, as `trait-parameters.tex:105-113` does, stay as they are. Qualify any other hit that states what an implementation does, in the same form as steps 1 to 3. On `6a654baa13` the grep finds no hit beyond those three.

5. Build the specification once, as `specification.md`, "Building it", says. If the gate is still running in this tree, start the build after the gate ends, so that nothing runs beside it. Do not read the gate's output. Both `./ant genSource` and `./ant tex` must end in `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, and the warning grep of that section must print 0. Then run `git clean -fXq -- Specification`. Quote two to five lines of each result in your report, with the command that printed them.

6. Commit the three edited `.tex` files locally on `main`, in one commit, with the skill's footer (`committing.md`). The message says that the commit edits the original tree's specification, and that it names walk's halves of rows 968 and 962 in `revival-numerals`' Effect and qualifies the two boxes. Do not push.

7. Record the repair in `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-29/RECORD.md`, in the gather's section on the specification (the paragraph that cites the two builds). Add one sentence that names this commit, rows 962 and 968, and the build's two `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` lines. Commit that file after step 6, also locally.

The repair does not touch the routed items `review-routed.1` and `review-routed.2`. It adds no test (`specification.md`: an edit of the text has no test) and changes no ledger row: the review filed row 968 and noted rows 961 and 962 in `6a654baa13`.
